canonicalExplanation.summary: A **commit** records **the index**, not your whole folder. It stores a snapshot of the staged content, a pointer to its **parent** commit, **author and committer** names and times, and a **message**. Once made, it never changes; "editing" one really creates a new commit. `git commit` is **local**: nothing reaches GitHub until you push. The habit that makes commits useful: **stage one purpose, review `git diff --staged`, then commit with a message that says why**. Unrelated experiments stay unstaged for later.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner fixed a scoring bug and, while there, started renaming variables in another file. They run `git commit -am "stuff"` and later can't tell which line fixed the bug when a reviewer asks. A learner stages one bug fix, reviews the staged diff, commits it with a causal message, and leaves an unrelated experiment unstaged. In this lesson you'll produce a commit whose staged diff matches its stated purpose.

```predict
{"question": "You run `git commit` successfully. Is your work now on GitHub?", "options": ["Yes, commit uploads it", "No: commit is local; git push sends it to a remote"], "answer": 1, "why": "Commit writes to your local .git database. Pushing is a separate step (later module)."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Filesystem and terminal fluency** module, **Working tree, index and HEAD**, and **Ignore policy**.

sections.heading: The object: what a commit records
sections.body:
```bash
git status                     # score.js (fix) and names.js (experiment) modified.
git add score.js               # stage only the fix.
git diff --staged              # review: exactly the fix, nothing else.
git commit -m "Fix score total ignoring bonus points" \
  -m "The total skipped bonus because the loop started at index 1."
git show --stat HEAD           # the commit: message, author, one file changed.
git status                     # names.js still modified, uncommitted.
```

```text
commit 3f2a9c1   (snapshot of the index)
parent 8b7d0e4
Author: Asha <asha@example.com>
    Fix score total ignoring bonus points
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why avoid `git commit -am` here?", "answer": "-a stages every modified tracked file, so the experiment would ride along with the fix. Stage explicitly when a commit should have one purpose."}
```

examples.title: One fix, one commit
examples.situation: A learner stages one bug fix, reviews the staged diff, commits it with a causal message, and leaves an unrelated experiment unstaged.
walkthrough: **Stage one bug fix:** git add score.js stages only the fix; names.js stays modified.
**Review the staged diff:** git diff --staged shows just the bonus-loop change.
**Commit with a causal message:** "Fix score total ignoring bonus points"; git status will still show the unrelated experiment unstaged.
examples.result: The commit's staged diff matches its message, and the experiment waits for its own commit.

examples.title: The mystery commit
examples.situation: A teammate's commit titled "update" changes 14 files: a bug fix, formatting, a new dependency and half a feature.
walkthrough: Nobody can review or revert the bug fix alone.
Split work by purpose: stage the fix, commit; stage formatting, commit.
Use git add -p when one file mixes purposes.
examples.result: Each commit has one purpose, so reviewing and reverting are easy.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Commit saves the entire project exactly as currently visible and sends it to GitHub in one operation.
misconceptions.correction: A commit records only the staged index, not unstaged edits or untracked files, and it stays local until pushed.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "One fix, one commit", what happened to names.js?

analogy.example: A commit is like **a labelled, sealed photo in an album**. You choose what's in frame (staging), check the preview (diff --staged), write a caption (message), and it's glued in, pointing to the photo before it (parent). Sharing the album with friends (push) is a separate trip.
limitations: Photos show everything in frame; commits show only what you staged.
You can't edit a glued photo, only add a corrected one.

steps.explanation: The learner stages one bug fix only.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, change two files for different reasons. Commit them as two separate commits, each with a message that states why, and show both with git log --stat.
scaffold: Stage one file at a time.

farTransfer.prompt: Take a working tree with a bug fix, a formatting change in the same file and a new untracked file. Produce three purposeful commits using git add -p, verifying each staged diff before committing, and explain why the order you chose makes review easier.
scaffold: Formatting first or last, never mixed.
expectedEvidence: Three commits, each diff matches its message.
No unrelated change in any commit.

remediation.explanation: Before each commit say the purpose in one sentence, then check: **does git diff --staged contain exactly that, and nothing else?**

recap.summary: To produce a commit whose staged diff matches its purpose, stage only the related changes, review git diff --staged, commit with a message that explains why, and remember a commit stores the index snapshot, parent, author and message locally until pushed.
